This is a petition filed u/s.166 of Indian Motor Vehicles Act, by the petitioner Kadar Sharief A.,
claiming for grant of compensation of Rs.30,00,000/- for the injuries sustained by him in the accident on 16.06.2021.
Thereafter, during the trial, on 02.10.2022 petitioner reported to be dead and petitioner counsel has filed the application on IA No.I and II to bringing the LR's on record.

Accordingly, petitioner No.1(A) to (D) being the wife and children of the deceased petitioner were brought on record and were permitted to continue the proceedings.
2.

The petitioner's case in brief as follows:
On 18.03.2021 at about 17:15 to 17:20 pm, the petitioner/deceased was riding a motor cycle bearing Reg. No.KA-05-KT-1568 and when he reached near Donbosco collage, on BM Road, Kumbalagudu Village, Kengeri Hobli, Bengaluru city, at that time, suddenly the driver of Tipper Lorry bearing Reg. No.AP-16-TJ-4331 in a rash and negligent manner without observing any traffic rules and regulations dashed against the petitioner's Motor cycle.
Due to this impact, the petitioner/deceased fell down along with motorcycle and sustained grievous injuries all over the body.

Immediately petitioner was shifted to Rajarajeshwari Hospital, wherein he took first aid treatment and then shifted to St. Jhon's Hospital wherein he took treatment as an Kadar Sharief .A vs National Ins Co Ltd on 5 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/161368171/
2 inpatient and later shifted to SAFA Hospital wherein also treated as an inpatient and then shifted to Shifaa Hospital, Shivajinagar and again shifted to St. Jhon's Hosptial wherein he took treatment as an inpatient and discharged with an advice of complete bed rest and regular follow-up treatment.

3. After service of notice to respondents, the respondent No.2 remained exparte.

The respondent No.1 filed written statement wherein contended that there is a violation of Section 134(c) and 158(6)
of MV Act.

The driver of the Lorry bearing Reg. No.AP-16-TJ-4331 was not holding valid and effective driving licence and was also not having valid RC, FC and Permit to the vehicle and there was delay of 2 days in filing the complaint.
Further submitted that the Tipper lorry was falsely implicated by the petitioner colluding with the owner of the vehicle, hospital authorities and the police to get the compensation.
The petitioner himself was solely responsible for the alleged accident.
The driver of the respondent vehicle was not at all responsible for the cause of accident.

Further, respondent No.2 owner of the insured vehicle was allowed the vehicle to drive which driving by the driver who was not holding the valid and effective driving licence to drove the particular class of vehicle as on the date of accident.
Hence the owner of the vehicle committed breach of terms and conditions of the policy and hence this respondent No.1 is not at all liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.
Even the offending vehicle was not having the valid Permit and FC.
Hence, Respondent No.1 is not liable to pay any compensation.
Hence prays to dismiss the petition.

4. On the basis of the above pleadings this tribunal has framed the following issues :
ISSUES 1) Whether the petitioner prove that he has sustained grievous injuries in an accident that was occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of the Tipper bearing Reg. No.AP-16-TJ-4331 on 18.03.2021 at about 5.15 to 5.20 p.m., near BM Road, Donbosco College, Dumbalagudu Village, Kengeri Hobli, Bengaluru?
2) Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
If so, how much and from whom?

3) What order or award ?

By considering the nature of injuries sustained by the petitioner/deceased and treatment taken by him and duration of his stay in the St. John's Medical College hospital as inpatient from 18.03.2021 to 22.03.2021 for a period of 5 days and then taken treatment at Shifaa Hospital as an inpatient from 15.04.2021 to 22.04.2021 for a period of 8 days and then taken treatment at St. John's Medical College hospital as inpatient from 22.04.2021 to 12.05.2021 for a period of 21 days, total for the period of 34 days petitioner has taken treatment as an inpatient, it is quite natural that petitioner could not have carried out his avocation for at least 6 months.

Further, RW.1 clearly stated that he has given notice under Sec.133 of IMV Act to the owner of the vehicle to produce the documents and he has received the reply from the RC owner along with the RC, DL, Insurance and Permit.

On perusal of which,
it clearly shows that the vehicle bearing Reg. No.AP-16-TJ- 4331 was permitted to run in all routes in Andhra Pradesh state except prohibited.

As per FIR, complaint and the charge sheet, the accident has been taken place in the Mysore-Bengaluru Highway near Don-Bosco College, Kumbalgod Village, Kengeri Hobli, Bengaluru i.e., within the limits of Karnataka State.
Thus it appears that as on the date of accident, the offending vehicle was not having valid permit to drive in Karanataka.
Thus the owner of the offending vehicle respondent No.2 has violated the terms of the policy.

Though RW.1 was cross examined by petitioner counsel, but, RW.1 categorically denied the suggestion made by the petitioner counsel that he is deposing falsely that the offending vehicle was not having valid permit to drive in Karnataka.
From Ex.R.1, it is clear that the offending vehicle was not having valid permit to drive in the Karnataka as on the date of accident and respondent No.2 has violated the terms of the policy.

However, this court held that even if the insurer succeeds in establishing its defence, the Tribunal or the court can direct the insurance company to pay the award amount to the claimant(s)
and in turn, recover the same from the owner of the vehicle.
The three Judge Bench after analyzing the earlier decisions on the point, held that there was no reason to deviate from the said well settled principle.

31. In the case of third party risks, as per the decision in National Insurance Company Ltd. v.
Swaran Singh the insurer had to indemnify the compensation amount payable to the third party and the insurance company may recover the same from the insured.

sentences.text: Doctrine of "pay and recover" was considered by the Supreme Court in Swaran Singh case wherein the Supreme Court examined the liability of the insurance company in cases of breach of policy condition due to disqualifications of the driver or invalid driving licence of the driver and held that in case of third party risks, the insurer has to indemnify the compensation amount to the third party and the insurance company may recover the same from the insured.

Elaborately considering the insurer's contractual liability as well as statutory liability vis-a-vis the claims of third parties, the Supreme Court issued detailed guidelines as to how and in what circumstances, "pay and recover" can be ordered.

In para (110), the Supreme Court summarised its conclusions as under:-
"110.

The summary of our findings to the various issues as raised in these petitions is as follows:
(i) Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 providing compulsory insurance of vehicles against third-party risks is a social welfare legislation to extend relief by compensation to victims of accidents caused by use of motor vehicles.
The provisions of compulsory insurance coverage of all vehicles are with this paramount object and the provisions of the Act have to be so interpreted as to effectuate the said object.

(ii) An insurer is entitled to raise a defence in a claim petition filed under Section 163-A or Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, inter alia, in terms of Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the said Act.

(iii) The breach of policy condition e.g. disqualification of the driver or invalid driving licence of the driver, as contained in sub-section (2)(a)(ii) of Section 149, has to be proved to have been committed by the insured for avoiding liability by the insurer.

Mere absence, fake or invalid driving licence or disqualification of the driver for driving at the relevant time, are not in themselves defences available to the insurer against either the insured or the third parties.

To avoid its liability towards the insured, the insurer has to prove that the insured was guilty of negligence and failed to exercise reasonable care in the matter of fulfilling the condition of the policy regarding use of vehicles by a duly licensed driver or one who was not disqualified to drive at the relevant time.

sentences.text:
(iv) Insurance companies, however, with a view to avoid their liability must not only establish the available defence(s) raised in the said proceedings but must also establish "breach" on the part of the owner of the vehicle;
the burden of proof wherefore would be on them, (v) The court cannot lay down any criteria as to how the said burden would be discharged, inasmuch as the same would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

(vi) Even where the insurer is able to prove breach on the part of the insured concerning the policy condition regarding holding of a valid licence by the driver or his qualification to drive during the relevant period, the insurer would not be allowed to avoid its liability towards the insured unless the said breach or breaches on the condition of driving licence is/are so fundamental as are found to have contributed to the cause of the accident.

The Tribunals in interpreting the policy conditions would apply "the rule of main purpose"
and the concept of "fundamental breach" to allow defences available to the insurer under Section 149(2) of the Act.

(vii) The question, as to whether the owner has taken reasonable care to find out as to whether the driving licence produced by the driver (a fake one or otherwise), does not fulfill the requirements of law or not will have to be determined in each case.

(viii) If a vehicle at the time of accident was driven by a person having a learner's licence, the insurance companies would be liable to satisfy the decree.
32.

Applying the ratio laid down in the aforesaid ruling to the facts of the present case, admittedly petitioner is a third party to the contract between respondent No.1 and 2 and respondent No.2 is the owner of the offending vehicle

and it is not even proved that there is a fraud played by the petitioner in collusion with respondent No.1 and respondent No.2/owner of the offending vehicle in order to get wrongful gain to themselves and wrongful loss to the insurer.

33. Under the given circumstances this court finds, it just to order the respondent No.1 to pay the compensation amount to the petitioner and then to recover the said amount from the respondent No.2 under pay and recovery theory.

Hence by fastening liability on the respondent No.1, this court directs the respondent No.1 to pay compensation to the petitioner along with interest at 6 % p.a.
from the date of accident till the date of deposit of entire amount and then to recover the said amount from the respondent No.2.

Hence this issue No.2 is answered as 'Partly in the Affirmative'.

opennyai_summary.facts:
The respondent No.1 filed written statement wherein contended that there is a violation of Section 134(c) and 158(6)
of MV Act.
The driver of the Lorry bearing Reg. No.AP-16-TJ-4331 was not holding valid and effective driving licence and was also not having valid RC, FC and Permit to the vehicle and there was delay of 2 days in filing the complaint.
The driver of the respondent vehicle was not at all responsible for the cause of accident.
Further, respondent No.2 owner of the insured vehicle was allowed the vehicle to drive which driving by the driver who was not holding the valid and effective driving licence to drove the particular class of vehicle as on the date of accident.
Hence the owner of the vehicle committed breach of terms and conditions of the policy and hence this respondent No.1 is not at all liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.
Even the offending vehicle was not having the valid Permit and FC.
Hence, Respondent No.1 is not liable to pay any compensation.
opennyai_summary.issue:

No.AP-16-TJ-4331 on 18.03.2021 at about 5.15 to 5.20 p.m., near BM Road, Donbosco College, Dumbalagudu Village, Kengeri Hobli, Bengaluru?

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The very manner of the accident clearly shows that the accident has been taken place due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending vehicle.
Even respondent No.1 has not examined the driver of offending vehicle who is the material witness to disprove the contention of petitioner or to prove their defence.
Even the petitioner has not examined doctor to prove that the injuries sustained by the petitioner have let to the death of petitioner.
Even no follow-up medical documents have been produced to show that the petitioner was taking follow-up treatment till his death and due to the injuries sustained by him, he has succumbed.
Hence in the absence of any evidence and documents, merely on the self- serving statement of the PW.1, this court cannot assess the cause of death and come to the conclusion that the petitioner died due to the injuries sustained in the hospital.
It is a ordinary prudent of a common prudent man that if a person at first sustained injury and then because of the injuries has breathed his last then same has will be intimated to the jurisdictional police and thereafter further complaint will be lodged.
In the instant case on hand the non action of PW.1 itself vibrantly goes to show that, there is absolutely no nexus with the injuries with that of the death of the petitioner.
Absolutely no iota of evidence is placed on record to prove that the deceased died on account of injuries sustained in the accident.
There is no documents to prove the income of the deceased petitioner.

(ii) An insurer is entitled to raise a defence in a claim petition filed under Section 163-A or Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, inter alia, in terms of Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the said Act.
(iii) The breach of policy condition e.g. disqualification of the driver or invalid driving licence of the driver, as contained in sub-section (2)(a)(ii) of Section 149, has to be proved to have been committed by the insured for avoiding liability by the insurer.
Mere absence, fake or invalid driving licence or disqualification of the driver for driving at the relevant time, are not in themselves defences available to the insurer against either the insured or the third parties.
To avoid its liability towards the insured, the insurer has to prove that the insured was guilty of negligence and failed to exercise reasonable care in the matter of fulfilling the condition of the policy regarding use of vehicles by a duly licensed driver or one who was not disqualified to drive at the relevant time.
